---
title: "Iteration Patterns"
unit: 2
cluster: "Working with Lists"
---

A `for` loop can go over more than the elements of one list. This lesson
collects the common patterns: iterating over a list, over a sequence of
numbers, over two lists together, and over the index and the element together.
Each pattern can be written as a loop or as a list comprehension.

In this lesson, we'll learn how to:

* iterate over a sequence of numbers with `range()`
* iterate over two lists together with `zip()`
* iterate over the index and the element together with `enumerate()`

**The pattern decides what the loop goes over: a list, `range()`, `zip()` of
two lists, or `enumerate()` of a list. The loop and the comprehension work the
same way for all of them.**

## Iterating over a list

The loop variable takes each element of the list in turn:

```{python}
words = ["red", "green", "blue"]

for word in words:
    print(word, word.upper())
```

The list comprehension form builds a list from the same elements:

```{python}
[word.upper() for word in words]
```

## Iterating over a sequence of numbers

The built-in `range()` function produces a sequence of numbers. `range(5)`
produces the numbers from `0` up to, but not including, `5`. The `list()`
function converts the sequence into a list, so that we can see the numbers:

```{python}
list(range(5))
```

A loop can go over the sequence directly, without converting it:

```{python}
for i in range(5):
    print(i, i * i)
```

The list comprehension form:

```{python}
[i * i for i in range(5)]
```

`range()` can also take a start and a stop. Like a slice, the start is included
and the stop is not:

```{python}
list(range(1, 6))
```

## Iterating over two lists together

Two lists can hold related values in the same order. This list has the years
from 2016 to 2025, made with `range()`:

```{python}
years = list(range(2016, 2026))
years
```

This list has the annual rainfall in Bangalore for those years, in
millimetres:

```{python}
rainfall = [791, 1696, 618, 960, 1213, 1511, 1958, 1020, 1154, 1045]
```

The figures are measured by the India Meteorological Department (IMD), from the
[Bengaluru rainfall dataset](https://data.opencity.in/dataset/bengaluru-rainfall)
published by OpenCity.

The two lists are in the same order: the first rainfall figure belongs to the
first year. The built-in `zip()` function pairs the elements of two lists:
the first with the first, the second with the second, and so on. A loop over
`zip()` has two loop variables, one for each list:

```{python}
for year, mm in zip(years, rainfall):
    print(year, mm)
```

Each time the loop runs, `year` is an element of `years` and `mm` is the
element of `rainfall` at the same position.

The list comprehension form can use both variables. This one finds the years
with more than 1500 mm of rain:

```{python}
[year for year, mm in zip(years, rainfall) if mm > 1500]
```

## Iterating over the index and the element together

Sometimes a loop needs the position of each element as well as the element.
The built-in `enumerate()` function pairs each element with its index:

```{python}
chapters = ["List Indexing", "List Slicing", "Sorting Lists", "Modifying Lists"]

for i, title in enumerate(chapters):
    print("Chapter", i, title)
```

The index starts at `0`. To start counting from `1`, pass `start=1`:

```{python}
for i, title in enumerate(chapters, start=1):
    print("Chapter", i, title)
```

`start=1` changes only the numbers that `enumerate()` produces. The elements
are the same.

The list comprehension form can build a numbered title for each chapter. `str()`
converts the number to a string, so that it can be joined to the title with
`+`. The result is printed with `print()` because it is too long to display on
one line:

```{python}
print([str(i) + ". " + title for i, title in enumerate(chapters, start=1)])
```

## Practice

### Problem 1

Write a loop that prints the numbers from `1` to `10` and the cube of each
number, one pair per line:

```text
1 1
2 8
3 27
...
10 1000
```

### Problem 2

Write a function `vector_add` that adds two lists of numbers element by
element:

```python
>>> vector_add([1, 2, 3, 4], [10, 20, 30, 40])
[11, 22, 33, 44]
>>> sum(vector_add([1, 2, 3, 4], [10, 20, 30, 40]))
110
```

### Problem 3

Complete the following program by replacing each `___` with appropriate code.
It prints a numbered list of the cities, starting from `1`.

```python
cities = ["Bengaluru", "Chennai", "Mysuru"]

for ___ in ___:
    print(i, city)
```

When executed, the program produces the following output:

```text
1 Bengaluru
2 Chennai
3 Mysuru
```

### Problem 4

Using `years` and `rainfall` from this lesson, write a list comprehension that
gives the years with less than 1000 mm of rain.

## Summary

| Form or rule | Meaning |
|--------------|---------|
| `for word in words:` | iterates over the elements of a list |
| `range(5)` | the numbers `0`, `1`, `2`, `3`, `4` |
| `range(2016, 2026)` | the numbers from `2016` up to, but not including, `2026` |
| `list(range(5))` | converts the sequence into the list `[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]` |
| `for year, mm in zip(years, rainfall):` | iterates over two lists together, one element from each |
| `for i, title in enumerate(chapters):` | iterates over the index and the element together |
| `enumerate(chapters, start=1)` | counts the index from `1` instead of `0` |
| `[str(i) + ". " + title for i, title in enumerate(chapters, start=1)]` | a comprehension over the index and the element together |
| `[i * i for i in range(5)]` | a comprehension over a sequence of numbers |
| `[year for year, mm in zip(years, rainfall) if mm > 1500]` | a comprehension over two lists together |

And the one idea to carry forward: choose what the loop goes over. A list,
`range()`, `zip()` and `enumerate()` all work the same way in a loop and in a
list comprehension.
